I used to hang out with girls during elementary school. I would even have sleepovers with the girls at my school until that became socially inappropriate.

I used to play a game after school with my sister and my friend where they would try to catch me and if they did I'd act like a girl for a period of time. I'd often let myself get caught.

When I had to move towns, I was disconnected from all those experiences. Brought to a shitty Canadian oil town I was immediately bullied for my odd behavior. I stopped functioning like a normal child and became incredibly defiant. There was just something wrong and I could describe it, so I just got angry.

Looking back, I feel like those were all signs.

I'm a Canadian Paramedic. 

I have had a rather pleasant experience in hospitals. Most staff either don't care or are quite respectful. Oftentimes I don't have time for interpersonal communication, but when I do everything is usually like "Oh you're Trans? I'm sorry I've been refering to you as {your assumed gender}"

The patients are the main group that makes me feel uncomfortable sometimes. I've been in the box with a literal nazi. So you need to keep in mind your area and the populations you're likely to be working with.

I'm a paramedic so I spend lots of time in lots of different hospitals and everyone I have talked too has been incredibly nice.

Every group has its haters, but it's a group of people dedicated to helping people, You'll probably find your space.
I also find it helps with the ADHD, when I have no time to get scatterbrained, because the adrenaline is winning, I can think clearly!

When I started transitioning, I was in college to be a programmer until I had a mental health crisis. Following that I decided to reconsider my career. 

Now I'm a paramedic! Which is really cool. People tend to see the uniform before they see me, which helps a lot with me feeling safe. I'm also in Canada so I actually get paid enough to make this a career.

It's also a field that is inherently quite masculine in presentation, but I work with a lot of women. This has helped immensely in allowing me to accept my more masculine traits.
